title: Charlie Parker and the pro-rated contract
summary: Cobb recalls that Parker, paid $1,750 a week at Birdland, often failed to show until his contract was pro-rated.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Now, it is too bad, because he's got a lot of talent, but there's no question that he upset people unnecessarily.

I'm going to -- y @h, Stanley, may I say something to you? Charlie Parker was one of the greatest guys on an instrument. And Birdland was named after him. They'd call him Bird, Yardbird, you see. So they named Birdland after him. We all worked downtown, and Charlie would come in late some nights. Some nights he wouldn't show. And he had a contract like $1,750.00 a week for himself. And he worked for somebody else.

And one time he worked for my rhythm section, which they had to get paid double for the week. So they made two week's salary in one week. But what they had to finally do with Charlie is pro-rate his contract. The nights he didn't show, he didn't get paid. So that -- then, fine, if he showed, okay, you get paid. If you don't show -- but when they started pro-rating his contract, he showed immediately, if not sooner. See the difference?

Right. So this is a source of punishment due to -- like I told you, I got (inaudible). But when he wasn't showing, they were still giving him his money because he was Yardbird. Then they started to take it out of his salary when he didn't show, he didn't like that. So that made
him show a little more often than he was doing. Always a way to ship the mule, isn't it?
I'm with you now, Mr. Dance.
They had a lot of trouble with him (inaudible).
